items.t: Cross‐sectoral collaboration in times of crisis: Comparing the Czech Republic , Slovakia , and Poland
items.abs: The Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Poland, with their shared political histories, have confronted the compounded challenges of the COVID‐19 pandemic and the Ukraine war. These difficulties spurred the emergence of public–nonprofit collaboration in all three countries, each taking distinct paths. Our study aims to unravel these divergent trajectories of public–nonprofit collaboration through the lens of historical institutionalism. Using this lens, we attribute this divergence to the influence of the broader institutional environment, whose evolution has followed distinct trajectories in the examined countries. To achieve our objectives, we employed single‐country case study methods, leveraging desk research and structured interviews with management informants from nonprofit organizations in the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Poland (37 respondents in total). Our study demonstrates that the perceptions of the institutional environment by nonprofit actors directly shape the effectiveness of collaborations between the public sector and nonprofit organizations. Contrary to Western expectations, our findings challenge the seemingly prevailing optimism regarding the outcomes of public–nonprofit collaboration and emphasize the influence of factors such as path dependency, mutual distrust, and prior negative experiences.

items.t: The impact of self-reinforcing and self-undermining policy feedback on Mexican social policy: the end of the conditional cash transfer programme
items.abs: The conditional cash transfer programme (CCT) for poor families was terminated in Mexico in 2019. CCTs seek to fight poverty under a social investment logic by promoting the formation of human capital through the compliance of behavioural conditionalities. The programme – the first of its kind introduced at national level – accomplished several achievements and was maintained and developed by three successive federal administrations. As the backbone of anti-poverty policy for more than two decades, its achievements included delivering positive results to a significant proportion of the population; and triggering the expansion of social policy beyond social insurance. As a result, it was emulated by governments across the globe. A programme of these characteristics would have been expected to generate path dependency and policy stability, yet it was swiftly terminated with practically no opposition. This article applies a framework of historical institutionalism to analyse the feedback effects developed during the duration of the programme from the perspectives of beneficiaries, in order to contribute to the explanation of its termination. The research is based on qualitative empirical data from interviews with former beneficiaries. Our findings show that self-undermining mechanisms linked to a ‘hard’ design and implementation of conditionalities counterbalanced the self-reinforcing mechanisms derived from the benefits supplied by the programme, causing beneficiaries to become apathetic towards its continuity or termination. Conclusions yield theoretical insights that might serve to examine policy feedback in similar contexts, as well as lessons for policymakers regarding the design and implementation of social programmes.

items.t: Examining municipalities’ choices of service delivery modes through the lens of historical institutionalism
items.abs: While the motives behind municipalities’ choices of service delivery modes may lie in the past, current research still pays little attention to history. Applied to the service delivery of two waste services in nine municipalities over the period 1962–2021, this study aims to overcome this limitation by bringing in historical institutionalism. Based on the analysis of a database covering 4,599 government documents and 30 semi-structured interviews, we show that past choices structure future choices by creating juridical and economic lock-ins. Path-dependent processes overrule other potential sources of change in choices, resulting in a high degree of stability of choices.

items.t: The evolutionary trajectory of social enterprises in the Czech Republic and Slovakia
items.abs: The paper contributes to the research on social enterprises. Based on historical institutionalism, we map the evolution of social enterprises in the Czech Republic and Slovakia after the collapse of communist rule. The findings indicate that the historical-evolutionary trajectories differ, despite their common path during the totalitarian regime. There is some convergence based on significant political changes that resulted mostly in the need to create integrated legislation and to reflect the common European policy; the divergent trends occur after exogenous economic shocks, the effects of which might result from the differing initial macroeconomic situations in both countries.

items.t: Australian Quarantine Policy: From Centralization to Coordination with Mid‐Pandemic COVID‐19 Shifts
items.abs: Combining a historical institutionalism approach with institutional isomorphism and punctuated equilibrium, this article analyzes quarantine policy change across 120 years of Australian quarantine history. By anchoring its analysis within specific time periods (the years before the Spanish flu, seven decades of inaction, and multiple post-1997 pandemic updates and responses), the authors highlight when and why policies did or did not change and how the constant push-and-pull between state and Commonwealth institutional ownership altered policy possibilities. The heart of the analysis showcases how Australia's successful COVID-19 response is a unique output of prior quarantine policies, institutional evolution, and mid-pandemic alterations of key national pandemic response plans.

items.t: From path dependence to policy mixes for Nordic electric mobility: Lessons for accelerating future transport transitions
items.abs: We examine the problem of how to accelerate policies related to electric vehicles (EVs) in the Nordic countries Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden. These four Nordic countries represent an interesting collection of cases by virtue of having common decarbonization targets extending to the transport sector, interlinked electric energy systems and a joint electricity market largely based on low-carbon energy while they are open societies bent on innovation, making them well adaptable to a transition toward electric mobility. Our analytical framework drawing from transition research, lock-in and path dependency and institutionalism enables us to discern technological, institutional and behavioral mechanisms which can have both constraining and enabling effects vis-à-vis this transition by means of shaping national socio-technical systems and regimes. On this basis, we also discuss how to develop policies accelerating the transition. We find that the incumbent industries can shape policy choice through the lock-in into institutional inter-dependencies. The accumulation of social and material features, and vested interests of actors, for its part can maintain regime level inertia, impeding the transition. Yet, technological lock-in can also enable EVs, by means of learning effects from technologically interrelated wind energy projects and available infrastructure in buildings that support the EV charging needs. Overall, the complexity of path-dependent mechanisms embedded in the dominant regimes, together with the diversity of emerging policy mixes, demands attention both on the technologies and broader socio-technical systems in order to properly assess the prospects of transition toward electric mobility.

items.t: Why Some Critical Junctures Lead Nowhere: Exploring Dynamic and Static Policy Paths
items.abs: Some critical junctures fail to cause significant change in practice. Inspired by historical institutionalism, this article develops the concept of dynamic and static policy paths to explain why some critical junctures do not lead to change, while others do. Combining insights from policy process literature and policy implementation, it conceptualizes critical junctures through four elements: framing, targets, instruments, and actors/institutions. Based on two case studies, the article argues that the importance of framing and targets has been overexaggerated, and that a dynamic path will not occur unless there is also a significant change in instruments and actors/institutions. In Denmark, a climate policy agreement created a new policy direction for agriculture in which climate policy is a key component. In Norway, a climate policy agreement did not change the trajectory of sectoral policy and climate policy development has remained stagnant. Thus, differences in the critical junctures led to different policy paths.

items.t: What Agencies Post vs. What the Public Engages With: A CERC Analysis of Crisis Messaging on X During the 2025 Los Angeles Wildfires
items.j: Journal of Contingencies and Crisis Management
items.abs: This study examines official crisis communication on X during the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires through the Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC) framework. Using a human‐coded content analysis of 973 posts from 13 official institutional accounts, messages were classified by communication type and mapped across the crisis lifecycle: pre‐crisis, initial, maintenance, resolution, and evaluation. The presence of crisis‐related information was analyzed, as was whether posts were primarily instructive or reassuring/empathetic. Audience engagement was also assessed by using platform‐generated metrics, including likes, retweets, and replies. Frequency of communication peaked during the initial and maintenance stages and was dominated by informational and instructive content. However, the messages that generated the strongest public response were not the most common. Welch's ANOVAs revealed that reassuring and empathetic posts received significantly more likes (nearly twice the average of instructive posts) and replies than instructive posts, despite being used less frequently. By comparing what agencies posted most against what audiences engaged with most across the crisis lifecycle, this study identifies a disconnect between wildfire message strategy and public response, offering practical insights for improving emergency communication on social media.

items.t: The dialectics of menopause inequity: Intersections of normalising and pathologising discourses of menopause in migrant domestic workers’ narratives
items.abs: This paper focuses on a dialectic interplay of systemic and discursive inequities in the menopause experience of Filipino migrant domestic workers (MDWs) in Hong Kong. Drawing on theme-oriented discourse analysis, the paper examines interviews with 15 MDWs to reveal the tensions between discursive constructions of menopause as simultaneously “normal” and “difficult.” Normalising menopause as an expectable reproductive milestone with relatively mild symptoms serves as a protective strategy, enabling women not to let it affect their employment. However, it hinders timely access to healthcare and reinforces menopause inequity. The pathologising discourse of “difficult” menopause is confined to the women’s immediate social networks of other females; these females serve as sources of information and social support. Pathologising narratives display the women’s high levels of menopausal literacy and symptoms that warrant clinical attention. We argue that addressing health inequities, including linguistic inequities, involves more than attention to systemic barriers and available linguistic resources. It requires attention to discursive processes through which health experiences and inequities are negotiated, reproduced, or resisted.

items.t: Expert knowledge dissemination online: Discursive choices, roles enacted and authorial voice constructed
items.abs: A wide range of digital practices are currently employed to disseminate specialised knowledge beyond expert communities. Expert knowledge needs to be recontextualised so that it becomes accessible, understood an acceptable to diversified audiences with varying levels of expertise. How knowledge brokers construct and project their authorial voice plays a key role in this endeavour. This paper proposes a framework for analysing the construction of authorial voice in digital practices that recontextualise expert knowledge, based on the discursive choices made by knowledge brokers and the discursive roles enacted through them. The framework is applied to a corpus of 40 digital dissemination texts: 20 author-generated texts published in The Conversation and 20 writer-mediated research digests in two disciplines: Economy and Natural Sciences. Overall results show that Stance-taking and Comprehensibility roles are more prominent than Credibility and especially Engagement roles. Differences are observed in the Credibility roles enacted by knowledge producers versus mediators, and in Stance-taking across disciplines. The results offer insights into how expert knowledge is disseminated in trustworthy digital sources and can inform more critical consumption and production of such practices.

items.t: The Language of Democratic Resilience and Decline: A Comparative Study of Politicians’ Communication on Facebook in Sweden and Hungary
When ancestors speak: competing discourses on the repatriation of Indigenous Paiwan ancestral remains in Taiwan
items.abs: In 2023, Taiwan undertook its first international repatriation of Indigenous ancestral remains. However, this event was less a straightforward success than a consequence of complex discourse. This study examines the Taiwanese state’s official narrative surrounding the repatriation of Paiwan ancestral remains and contrasts it with a counternarrative articulated by Paiwan communities, as revealed through one-on-one interviews. Within the framework of Critical Discourse Analysis, the study draws on Halliday’s transitivity system to compare how agency is allocated to Paiwan ancestral remains across these narratives. The analysis reveals how state narrative constructs remains as passive objects of policy and diplomacy, whereas Paiwan narrative positions them as active agents, embodying ongoing presence and relational power. The study argues that repatriation practices, constrained by governmental agendas, risk limiting the potential for reconciliation, transitional justice, and decolonization. It also calls for the genuine recognition of Indigenous voices, knowledge systems, and the sacred balance between the living and the dead.

items.t: Communicating and Constructing Risk: Government and Public Interactions in Responding to Heat Risks
items.abs: Extreme heat is an increasingly important public-health and governance challenge, yet less is known about how public and governmental communication construct heat risk differently and how these communication processes evolve over time. Drawing on Hilgartner's taxonomy, this study compares 49,633 public-initiated messages from the Message Board for Leaders and 3,475 posts from official governmental Weibo accounts in China. Combining topic modeling, LIWC-based text analysis, and econometric models, we examine how heat risk is constructed in public and governmental texts, how heat-related communication varies across cities and over time, and how textual features and risk-construction intensity are associated with platform-observable communication outcomes. The findings show that public messages are more problem-solving and demand-oriented, whereas government posts are more prevention- and guidance-oriented. Public and governmental communication exhibit asymmetry in both the prevalence of textual features and their associations with governmental responsiveness and public engagement. At the city-year level, risk construction and communication effectiveness exhibit short-run inconsistency but adjust toward a long-run equilibrium relationship, suggesting that heat-risk communication is an adaptive process shaped through repeated public-government platform interactions.

items.t: The Democratic Cost of Pursuing Virality: A Study into Parliamentary Communications
items.abs: The transformation of parliamentarians into media producers has heightened concerns about emerging forms of political communication. This mixed-methods paper examines the strategies they employ to enhance their digital presence. Based on in-depth interviews, it shows that Brazilian parliamentarians believe that social media penalize them for posting about congressional matters, reporting that content about legislative work and constituency services receives little engagement online. Conversely, they view the production of antagonistic content and alignment with news cycles as essential to maintaining an engaging social media presence. A computational analysis of 4,5 million posts on Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter supports these evaluations: posts about congressional matters are associated with lower engagement metrics, while the use of antagonistic language increases them. The analysis further discusses pathways through which visibility is sustained at the intersection of platform incentives and communicative practices. In sum, this mixed-methods study demonstrates that the mediatization of politics has created perverse incentives for parliamentarians to downplay congressional activity and prioritize confrontations on social media, weakening accountability in ways that may resonate far beyond Brazil.

items.t: Words make worlds: The discursive construction of poverty in China’s digital sphere
items.abs: This paper explores how poverty is discursively framed on Chinese digital platform amid rising socioeconomic inequality and the expanding influence of public narratives on social media. Drawing on corpus-assisted discourse-historical approach, this study investigates discursive strategies in the most widely read poverty-related articles on WeChat and examines the way poverty is constructed. The results show that poverty discourse functions as a powerful legitimation tool that reinforce existing power relations by categorizing and stigmatizing the poor, individualizing the causes of poverty, and mitigating structural critique. Nevertheless, power dynamics are also negotiated and contested as resistance discourse emerges despite stringent content regulation. The findings further reveal how poverty discourse operates as a constitutive mechanism that shapes public cognition and emotional engagement, thereby influencing broader societal perceptions of poverty in China.

items.t: When diplomats go populist: the normalization of populist discourse in digital diplomacy
items.abs: This study investigates shifts in diplomatic communication by applying Critical Discourse Analysis to the social media presence of the current American ambassador to Israel on the platform X, with a focus on his posts related to the recent Israel-Gaza conflict. Using Wodak’s framework, which outlines six functions of “shameless normalization” of populist political discourse, the research analyzes rhetorical strategies employed by the American ambassador when addressing international institutions, the media, peace activists, and traditional allies. The analysis identifies a transition from formal institutional discourse to a more informal and transgressive communicative style, where traditional norms are increasingly challenged, and defamation and mockery frequently serve as main argumentative strategies. This type of discourse is a barrier to a constructive dialogue and promotes the normalization of exclusionary policies. The study concludes that political appointees integrate populist rhetoric into mainstream diplomatic discourse on social media, resulting in a hybrid form of digital diplomacy that prioritizes domestic political support over traditional diplomatic responsibilities.

items.t: “Listen to me”: Multimodal calibration of accountability and turn-claiming in Mandarin citizen-official encounters
Does Gender Budgeting Improve Women's Well‐Being, Equality, and Empowerment?
items.abs: The United Nations' fifth Sustainable Development Goal calls for gender equality and empowerment. Gender budgeting (GB) has been proposed as a potential mechanism to reduce gender disparities. This is a novel approach to budgeting that considers the impact of public spending on women and other underrepresented groups. Despite its growing popularity, spreading to over 80 countries since its launch in the 1980s, the effectiveness of GB remains less understood. This study tests whether GB has led to tangible improvements in women's well‐being, equality, and empowerment. We use an event study research design with staggered adoption to analyze data across 47 countries from 2000 to 2023. Our analyses of average and heterogeneous treatment effects reveal short‐ and long‐term impacts; notably, we find significant reductions in maternal mortality ratios and adolescent birth rates, as well as improvements in women's political empowerment.

items.t: A Public Values Framework for AI Governance: Evidence From US Federal AI Policymaking
items.abs: Governments at all levels are grappling with AI's implications for public administration. Because federal actions often establish the principles guiding wider governance efforts, this study asks how US federal AI policies reflect—or fail to reflect—core public values. Drawing on a dataset of US federal AI policies from 2020 to 2023, we systematically analyze the risks, harms, and governance strategies employed across government‐issued and enacted policy documents. Specifically, we analyze 120 discrete policy sections or subsections of federal laws and regulations, utilizing the parsing approach of the AI Governance and Regulatory Archive (AGORA), all of which regulate the operation of the government itself rather than private sector behavior. We develop a theoretical and empirical crosswalk linking AI‐related risks and harms to prominent public values. Results indicate that while values such as individual rights, the common good, and accountability are regularly invoked, additional guidance around public values like citizen engagement, workplace standards, and responsiveness may be necessary to prevent public value failure. The study further categorizes governance strategies in AI policy documents into regulatory, service‐based, and informational instruments, and finds that regulatory policies are most likely to engage with public values.

items.t: Responsible Algorithmization in the Public Sector: A “Natural Perspective” Based on Ethnographic Research in Regulation, Policing, and Healthcare
items.abs: Responsible algorithmization refers to the use of algorithms in the public sector while safeguarding public values. Approaches to responsible algorithmization suggested by the EU, OECD, and others depart from a rational perspective and highlight formal structures and procedures. This paper complements this perspective by adding a “natural perspective,” which emphasizes sense‐making and actual practices. This natural perspective is used for a set of ethnographic studies of algorithmization in three domains in the Netherlands: regulation, policing, and healthcare. Our findings show that algorithmization of government organizations is an emergent, political, open, and fragmented process, rather than, as assumed by rational approaches to responsible algorithmization, pre‐structured, neutral, closed, and simple. This means that rational approaches fall short of providing a comprehensive basis for establishing responsible algorithmization. We conclude that not only passive responsibility but also active responsibility for algorithmization in the public sector needs to be addressed to safeguard public values.

items.t: The Right Key for the Right Lock: How Government Response Methods and Demand Types Affect Citizen Satisfaction
items.abs: Faced with diverse and complex demands from citizens, the government has consistently sought ways to enhance its ability to respond. Metaphorically, citizens' needs can be viewed as locks, and the government requires keys to unlock them. Artificial intelligence (AI) is an innovative new key offering a fresh paradigm for unlocking the door to high citizen satisfaction. Drawing on government responsiveness theory, this study applies a 2 × 3 between‐subjects survey experiment to explore the impact of government response methods (traditional responses, AI‐enabled responses) and citizen demand types (consultation, complaint/help‐seeking, suggestions) on citizen satisfaction. Findings show that AI‐enabled government responses significantly increase citizen satisfaction compared to traditional approaches. Among demand types, consultation yields the highest satisfaction, while suggestion results in the lowest. Further, the satisfaction level is significantly influenced by the interaction effect between response method and demand type. Perceived fairness mediates the relationship between government responses and citizen satisfaction, with citizen participation experience having a moderating effect. This study offers new insights into increasing citizen satisfaction from the perspective of government responses. It reveals the content‐dependent nature of AI‐enabled government responses, helping the government create unique AI response strategies and enhance digital interaction with citizens.
